passage: Cores drilled from harbor breakwaters built two thousand years ago show that seawater percolating through the volcanic ash mortar dissolved glassy particles and grew interlocking aluminous crystals along the cracks. Modern portland concrete degrades along exactly those channels, because its binder is chemically finished once cured. To argue that the mortar was weakened over time by the crystals that had first sealed its cracks

To argue that the mortar was chemically finished at curing and survived on sheer thickness
correct_answer: To argue that the mortar was strengthened over time by the seawater that attacks modern binders
explanation: The passage traces seawater through the cracks, where it dissolves ash and grows crystals "for centuries," and ends by saying the material "did not merely withstand seawater but required it" — the claim in "To argue that the mortar was strengthened over time by the seawater that attacks modern binders." "weakened over time by the crystals that had first sealed its cracks" reverses the passage, in which continued crystal growth is the source of durability, not of decay. "shielded from seawater by a surface layer its own cracking destroyed" fails because no surface layer is described; the water is said to percolate through the mortar. "chemically finished at curing and survived on sheer thickness" fails because the text says of the ancient mixture that it "had never finished reacting" and attributes finished chemistry to modern portland concrete instead.
